C0.quote: extensive research on the design of voting systems for participatory budgeting
C0.note: Approximate proportional core for participatory budgeting and committee selection (voting on outcomes from voters' preferences).

C1.loc: 4. Main Result: Approximate Core, Theorem 4.1, p.7; 5. Committee Selection, Theorem 5.1, p.10
C1.quote: under Assumption 1, there exists a 6.24-approximate core solution.
C1.note: Main results are existence of outcomes in the gamma-approximate (proportional) core; algorithms (Algorithms 1-3) are constructive proof devices, and the conclusion says computational aspects are beyond scope, so AL not coded. Existence of LEO (a market-type Lindahl equilibrium, not a game) is a technical tool, so EQ not coded.

C2.1.value: preference profiles; preference order; ranking preferences; approval preferences
C2.1.loc: 2. Notations and Preliminaries, p.3; 5. Committee Selection, p.10

C2.2.loc: 2. Notations and Preliminaries, p.3; 5. Committee Selection, Def. 5.1-5.2 and Sec. 5.1, p.10
C2.2.quote: Note that both ranking and approval preferences may allow ties.
C2.2.note: General model: strict preference order over outcomes (Sec. 2: 'We assume that the order is strict'). Section 5: ranking preferences induced by an item ranking and approval preferences given by an approved set; preferences over committees may have ties (weak orders).

C2.3.quote: voters have ordinal preferences over combinations of projects
C2.3.note: Voters are attributed preferences (and, for approval preferences, utilities u_i(S)).

C2.4.quote: preference order ⪰i over O. We assume that the order is strict.
C2.4.note: The rule's argument is the agents' preference orders, applied directly; the abstract says participants 'submit ordinal preferences' but only to contrast the format with numerical utilities, not to state that submitted equals held preferences.

C4.1.note: For approval preferences, utility is the number of approved candidates in the committee and the preference is defined by it; the introduction also mentions utility gains in the (alpha,beta)-core.

C4.2.note: The term 'dichotomous preferences' or an equivalent is not used; the paper speaks of approval preferences/ballots.

C5.1.quote: Our main solution concepts are the core and the approximate core
C5.1.note: The proportional core is presented as a fairness concept for groups of voters and is the criterion in all main results.

C5.2.quote: a feasible outcome o∗ is in γ-approximate core if for every outcome
C5.2.note: Core counts agents preferring o to o* according to the preference profile given to the rule; no statement relating it to submission or held attitudes.

VOT.quote_behav: preference order ⪰i over O. We assume that the order is strict.
VOT.note: Voters' preferences are taken as given by the rule. In the LEO construction (Sec. 3.2, p.5) 'a voter selects her most preferred affordable outcome' under fictitious personalised prices; this is a proof device, not voting behaviour, so not coded as STRAT.

OTH.note: A revenue-maximising 'centralized producer' appears only in the Lindahl/LEO analytical construction (Sec. 3), not as an actor in the voting model.
